clue.text: Leonard has it, and I have; it's soothing

parts.note: Len is the usual short form of the name Leonard
taken as written
contracted, I have becomes I've, apostrophe dropped in the grid

explanation.surface: Leonard has got something, and so have I, and whatever it is calms the nerves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' and 'and' are joining words; 'I have' must be contracted, with the apostrophe dropped in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A lenitive is a medicine or remedy that eases pain, so the adjective describes anything that calms or relieves.

clue.text: Positively the last round, if a man is to be saved from drink

definitions.text: Positively the last round, if a man is to be saved from drink

parts.words: Positively the last round, if a man is to be saved from drink
parts.note: reads like a temperance pledge about the final round at the bar, but the drink is the sea and the round is a ring-shaped float thrown to someone overboard

explanation.surface: A drinker is urged to call it a night before alcohol ruins him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' and 'drink' suggest the pub; in fact the round is a buoyant ring and 'the drink' is slang for the sea. It is the last thing a drowning man can hope for.
explanation.definitionFit: A ring-shaped float thrown to someone in the water keeps them from drowning; it is literally a belt for life.

clue.text: Henry — of course

parts.note: Henry suggests a man's name said with assurance, but the clue means the Portuguese prince known by this title, and also anyone whose job is plotting a ship's course

explanation.surface: Someone confidently names Henry as the obvious answer.
explanation.walkthrough: Prince Henry of Portugal, patron of fifteenth-century voyages, is known by this epithet; 'of course' reads as 'naturally' but also describes the person who sets a vessel's course.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Henry of Portugal sponsored ocean voyages and bears this title; generally the word means someone who plans a ship's or aircraft's route.

clue.text: Strike one key and write a book

parts.note: to strike a typewriter's keys is to type
E is one of the musical keys

explanation.surface: A writer hits a single typewriter key and claims to have produced a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and write' joins the wordplay to the definition. The book is Herman Melville's first novel, set in the South Seas.
explanation.definitionFit: Typee is Herman Melville's 1846 novel based on his stay in the Marquesas Islands.

clue.text: Certificate for brooch revealed in a turn of the cloth

indicators.note: the brooch is shown sitting inside the turned-round title, so one piece goes within the other
a turn here means a turning round, so the clergyman's title is read backwards

parts.note: the cloth means the clergy, and Rev, short for Reverend, is a cleric's title
an ouch is an old word for a clasp or brooch set with jewels

explanation.surface: Someone gets a certificate for a brooch found in the folds of a turned piece of fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a turn of' reverses the clergyman's title, and 'revealed in' places the old word for a brooch inside it. 'the cloth' is the clergy, not fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: A voucher is a document that serves as evidence or entitles the holder to something, a kind of certificate.

clue.text: Featherweight ?

parts.note: looks like a boxing class, but also describes a small fowl that weighs next to nothing; the boxing class just below featherweight shares its name

explanation.surface: A one-word query about a boxer's weight class.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the double reading: a tiny breed of chicken is light and feathered, and in boxing the next class down from featherweight carries the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: A bantam is a miniature domestic fowl and also the boxing weight class lighter than featherweight.

clue.text: What happened to the invalid ?

parts.note: invalid suggests a sick person (stress on the first syllable), but read as in-VAL-id it means something legally void, such as a marriage that has been cancelled

explanation.surface: A concerned enquiry about the fate of someone who was ill.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'invalid' as the adjective meaning void: what happens to a marriage or contract declared void is that it is cancelled outright.
explanation.definitionFit: When a court declares a marriage or contract void from the start, the legal process is called this.

clue.text: Mr. Big of shipshape character

parts.note: Mr Big is a giant or very powerful person, and adding the adjective ending -ic to that word names the most famous liner ever sunk, hence shipshape character

explanation.surface: A tidy-minded boss runs everything in good order.
explanation.walkthrough: A giant of Greek myth gives the word for a huge or powerful figure; its adjective is also the name of the White Star liner, so the word has a ship-like character.
explanation.definitionFit: The Titans were giant gods of Greek myth, so the word describes any person of great size or power, and its adjective named a famous liner.

clue.text: Cause of damage is in one of nine

indicators.note: the word is sits inside the goddess, one piece placed within the other

parts.note: the Muses of Greek myth were nine sister goddesses of the arts
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something that causes damage turns up among a group of nine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' places the little word inside the goddess after her first letter; 'one of nine' relies on knowing there were nine Muses.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrong or careless use of something is what damages it, so improper handling is a cause of harm.

clue.text: Pranks, chases, &c.

definitions.meaning: to prank, in an old sense, is to dress up or decorate showily
to chase metal is to decorate it by engraving or embossing

explanation.surface: A list of mischief and pursuits, cut off with an et cetera.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are verbs here, not nouns: 'prank' once meant to deck out, and 'chase' means to ornament metal. '&c.' marks that other ways of decorating would do as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses mean decorates: dressing something up in finery, and ornamenting metal by engraving it.

clue.text: What price that heavy-handed piano quintet ?

definitions.text: What price that heavy-handed piano quintet ?

parts.words: What price that heavy-handed piano quintet ?
parts.note: asks the cost of a chamber piece, but read literally a quintet of heavy-handed piano sounds is ... musical sounds, which is also a sum of banknotes

explanation.surface: Someone asks how much a clumsily played piano quintet is worth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What price' points at money; a heavy-handed pianist pounds the keys, so five notes pounded out become banknotes worth five pounds each.
explanation.definitionFit: Banknotes of five-pound value are the price paid, and also, punningly, five musical notes pounded on a piano.

clue.text: See 10
Swiveller the oversleeper, not the Colonel

definitions.text: Swiveller the oversleeper, not the Colonel

parts.words: Swiveller the oversleeper, not the Colonel
parts.note: suggests a character who lies in bed late, but describes a swivelling wheel truck that runs over railway sleepers, spelt differently from the golfing Colonel of the same sound

explanation.surface: Picks out a lazy character from a novel rather than a military officer.
explanation.walkthrough: Dick Swiveller is a Dickens character, which is the false trail. Railway sleepers are the cross-beams under the track; the swivelling truck under a carriage passes over them. Colonel Bogey is the imaginary golf opponent, spelt -EY.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway truck that pivots under a locomotive or carriage has this name, a homophone of the golfing Colonel's.

clue.text: Classes of ironmongery ware, worse luck

definitions.meaning: hardware ranges stocked by an ironmonger, the 'lines' of goods sold
an expression of sympathy for misfortune, like 'tough luck'

explanation.surface: An ironmonger's stock list ends with a sigh about bad fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: An ironmonger is a hardware shop; a shop's 'lines' are its ranges of goods. 'Hard lines' is a dated British expression meaning bad luck.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardware product ranges are hard goods lines; separately the phrase is a British way of saying tough luck.

clue.text: The French clock of a bishop ?

parts.note: la is the feminine definite article in French
a timer is a clock that measures elapsed time

explanation.surface: A French timepiece belonging to a churchman.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugh Latimer was Bishop of Worcester, burnt at the stake in Oxford in 1555; the question mark admits he is one bishop among many.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugh Latimer was a sixteenth-century English bishop and Protestant martyr.

clue.text: Flower more than enough to cover a bald patch

definitions.text: Flower more than enough to cover a bald patch

parts.words: Flower more than enough to cover a bald patch
parts.note: a plant named for a friar's cowl, which would more than cover the shaved crown of his tonsure

explanation.surface: A bloom big enough to hide a man's baldness.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant's name describes its hooded flowers; a friar's cowl would easily cover the tonsure, the shaven patch on his head.
explanation.definitionFit: Aconite is commonly called by this name because its blue blooms resemble a friar's cowl.

clue.text: "Now - -the crimson petal, now the white'" (Tennyson)

parts.note: a quotation with its verb missing, the opening of a lyric from Tennyson's The Princess

explanation.surface: A line of Victorian verse with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The lyric in The Princess begins 'Now sleeps the crimson petal, now the white'; the missing word fills the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb meaning rests or slumbers completes Tennyson's line about flowers closing at night.

clue.text: That sly glance Dewy's girl took at the Irish boys ?

definitions.text: That sly glance Dewy's girl took at the Irish boys ?

parts.words: That sly glance Dewy's girl took at the Irish boys ?
parts.note: a sly glance is a peep, and Dick Dewy's sweetheart in Hardy is Fancy Day, so her glance is that of Day; the Irish boys are an eighteenth-century Ulster society

explanation.surface: A country girl casts a coy look at some Irish lads.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hardy's Under the Greenwood Tree, Dick Dewy courts Fancy Day. The Peep o' Day Boys were a Protestant secret society in eighteenth-century Ulster; the phrase itself means dawn.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means dawn, first light, and it named the Irish society of Peep o' Day Boys.

clue.text: 00500 in message from abroad, that's the lot

indicators.note: the figures are placed inside the telegram, one piece within the other

parts.note: a cable is a telegram, the usual way to send a message overseas
read as 0, 0 and 500: two zeros are two Os and 500 in Roman numerals is D

explanation.surface: A coded string of digits inside an overseas telegram reveals the whole thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the figures inside the telegram. Read the figures as 0, 0, 500, the last a Roman numeral, rather than one number.
explanation.definitionFit: 'The whole caboodle' is an idiom for everything, the entire collection.

clue.text: Eccentric chaps who spurn self-starters ?

parts.note: describes odd people, but also starting handles, which turn a car engine by hand and are not needed in cars with self-starting motors

explanation.surface: Oddballs who scorn go-getters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Self-starters' sounds like ambitious people but is the electric starter motor of a car; the hand-turned starting handle is what a car without one needs. 'Eccentric' also hints at engineering.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both odd, obsessive people and the hand-turned levers used to start old car engines.

clue.text: The playwright need not be temperamental to make them

definitions.text: The playwright need not be temperamental to make them

parts.words: The playwright need not be temperamental to make them
parts.note: a dramatist writes divisions of a play, and a temperamental person causes tantrums in public; the same word covers both

explanation.surface: A dramatist can produce something without being moody.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'make' these can mean writing parts of a play's acts, or throwing public tantrums, which is what a temperamental person does.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the divisions of a play and noisy public displays of temper.

clue.text: Aphrodite's isle be thy care

indicators.note: be is read as a command to the letters to become something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A line of verse urging that the goddess's island be your concern.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be' signals that the letters of THY CARE rearrange. The surface reads like poetry; the island off the Peloponnese is where Aphrodite came ashore in some versions of the myth.
explanation.definitionFit: Cythera is a Greek island associated with the cult of Aphrodite, who was said to have risen from the sea there.

clue.text: Give way — iron could be the remedy

definitions.text: Give way — iron could be the remedy

parts.words: Give way — iron could be the remedy
parts.note: to give way is to collapse, and a creased crushed fold in fabric is put right with a hot iron

explanation.surface: Advice that iron supplements could help someone who is breaking down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron' reads as a mineral tonic, but it is the household appliance that smooths creased fabric; the same word means to collapse.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to collapse or give way and to crease cloth, which an iron smooths out.

clue.text: Designated copper after a fashion

indicators.note: the coin's letter follows the fashion, coming after it in the answer

parts.note: a style is a fashion or mode
a copper is a penny, abbreviated d in old British money

explanation.surface: A police officer has been named in a fashionable manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' looks like a policeman or the metal; it is a penny coin, written d in pre-1971 British money. 'after' puts D at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To be styled is to be given a name or title, so designated.

clue.text: Full fig, Eve's

parts.note: full fig means complete dress, and Eve's would be a bride's set of clothes, with a nod to her fig leaf

explanation.surface: Eve dressed in nothing but a fig leaf, in full.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Full fig' is an old phrase for full dress; 'Eve's' plays on the first woman's fig leaf and on 'eve' as the wedding eve, when the bride's outfit is ready.
explanation.definitionFit: A bride's collection of clothes and linen gathered for her marriage is her complete wardrobe.

clue.text: Bucks sheltered a stricken deer here

definitions.text: Bucks sheltered a stricken deer here

parts.words: Bucks sheltered a stricken deer here
parts.note: Bucks reads as male deer but is Buckinghamshire, and the stricken deer is how the poet William Cowper described himself

explanation.surface: Male deer protect a wounded companion.
explanation.walkthrough: Bucks is short for Buckinghamshire, an English county. William Cowper called himself 'a stricken deer that left the herd' in The Task, and lived in this town.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet William Cowper lived for years in this Buckinghamshire town.

clue.text: After the starting gun, a shot for the finish

definitions.text: After the starting gun, a shot for the finish

parts.words: After the starting gun, a shot for the finish
parts.note: a shot sounds like gunfire but is a picture taken at the end of a close race

explanation.surface: A race from the starting pistol to a final gunshot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot' reads as another gunshot but is a camera picture; a race too close to call is decided by a photo finish.
explanation.definitionFit: A photograph taken at the line decides a close race, hence the photo finish.

clue.text: Vote for the swells ?

definitions.meaning: to ... for a candidate is to give them all one's votes
to fill out or puff up, as a cushion does

explanation.surface: An election appeal to back the posh set.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swells' looks like a noun for well-dressed toffs but is a verb: grows round. 'Plump' as voting means casting a single vote for one candidate.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to give one's vote wholly to one candidate, and also to grow rounder, fill out.

clue.text: Fish, with a round tongue

parts.note: the ling is a long sea fish of the cod family
a round thing, a ring, is the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: A fish served with a rounded tongue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the pieces; 'tongue' is language, not the organ.
explanation.definitionFit: A tongue is a language, and this word is an informal term for a foreign or specialist language.

clue.text: Stray beast redeemed, as was made plain

definitions.meaning: a stray animal is put in the pound, and once bought back it is formerly pounded

explanation.surface: A lost animal is reclaimed, as the clue says plainly.
explanation.walkthrough: A pound is an enclosure for stray animals; one released from it has been ex-pounded, formerly impounded. 'as was' links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: To expound is to set out and explain fully, so the past form means explained clearly; the first reading splits it as ex-pounded.

clue.text: Girls for " Tree " brand soft drinks promotion

parts.note: dry describes non-alcoholic drinks, as in the soft-drink brand Canada Dry
ads, advertisements, are a form of promotion

explanation.surface: A marketing campaign for a soft-drinks brand called Tree uses girls.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an advertising campaign with 'Tree' as a brand name; really the girls belong to the trees, as wood nymphs.
explanation.definitionFit: Dryads are nymphs of Greek myth who live in trees, female spirits of the woods.

clue.text: Tyne hope of a devoted apprentice

indicators.note: of is read as made of, so the answer is built out of the letters of the two words before it, rearranged

explanation.surface: A Tyneside lad hopes to become a dedicated apprentice.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is only 'of' (made of): TYNE HOPE rearranged. Old puzzles often signalled anagrams this lightly. 'Devoted' fits the religious sense, a new convert.
explanation.definitionFit: A neophyte is a beginner or novice, originally a newly baptised convert, so a learner devoted to a new faith or craft.
